review:
About to be delisted, but it will remain playable and even the multiplayer servers will stay on for a good while longer. And yes, I intend to put at least another 1000 hours into it.
I don't even like racing games -- I always want to like them, but there have been very few that actually clicked with me and the last one was almost thirty years ago; until this one. It's not really a racing game. It's an open world car collectathon where you can do pretty much whatever you want, as long as it's with your car. Paint it. Tune it. Drive around properly. Drive around improperly and wreck everything. Take really cool photos. And I guess you can also race it, yeah.

As of Today. Forza Horizon 4 has been officially Delisted in Steam.


Press F to Pay Respects to this amazing great game for the people who bought it.

[i]NOTE: This game is being delisted from stores on December 15, 2024 and will no longer be purchasable.
The TL;DR is that I wholeheartedly recommend picking up the Ultimate Edition before this happens, but if you'd like to hear my reasoning, keep reading.[/i]

I've never been a huge fan of the racing genre. Whether it's simulation or arcade, open world or track based, it's a genre that I haven't played more than a few hours of since the likes of Burnout Takedown and Need For Speed Underground 20+ years ago.
The only reason I picked this game up at all was due to its impending delisting, and figured I may as well try it since I bought it, right?

I loved Forza Horizon 4. 

No, seriously - I have played 90 hours of this game over the last few months, and with very few exceptions, have loved every minute spent here. I need to stress how unlikely it is for a game about cars to take just a few hours of my time before I get bored, let alone 90. This game absolutely oozes style, and is a genuine joy to play.

It helps that there's tons to do. The map is full of races (street races, dirt races, cross country), different types of open world challenges such as setting off speed cameras, drift zones, ramps/jumps, open world collectibles, short stories. I found it really easy to sink into a bit of a flow state, ping-ponging from one challenge to another as I explored the map.

For multiplayer, there's racing as you'd expect, but there's also party modes akin to infection, capture the flag, etc. 
There is even a [b][i]literal Battle Royale mode[/i][/b] that was surprisingly well realized. These modes may not be everyone's cup of tea (especially the BR mode - you'll find opinions are mixed on this one), but they were a very pleasant surprise when I found them, and I enjoyed them a lot.

Technical performance was fantastic all the way through. The game runs like a dream, looks great, no bugs or crashes in my entire playthrough. It is an excellent PC port.

The Ultimate Edition includes two DLC expansions as well - Fortune Island and LEGO Speed Champions - and they are both really high quality. The LEGO one in particular is extremely dense, with lots to do, and really doubles down on the charm and style the rest of the game has. You can tell the team had an absolute blast making the LEGO content, and that excitement is likely to rub off on you as you play.
This is why, in my opinion, the Ultimate Edition is a must if you are going to pick this up.

I really strongly recommend this to anyone who has even a passing interest in trying a well made open world racing game.

Since the game will soon be removed from the store, here’s my two cents for those who collect great games.

Gameplay - Classic arcade racing with a mix of completely unnecessary simulator elements. The tracks are diverse, the variety of modes is extensive, there are tons of cars, the open world is vast and exploring it is extremely enjoyable, and the changing seasons (1 week per season) give the game world a unique feel. The only downside is the fine-tuning of cars, which comes straight from simulators, and here’s why:

1) Considering the huge number of cars, adjusting each one down to the millimeter can quickly become tiresome, especially when playing on the highest difficulty. Moreover, changing a parameter by just 0.1 can turn a car into a race machine, which feels unrealistic and makes me even less inclined to figure it out. Thankfully, there’s an option to load settings from other players, which is much appreciated.

2) If the game claims to be realistic, then why are crucial aspects like ground resistance missing? Without checkpoints, everyone would drive on the dirt road, regardless of whether you have a Bugatti Veyron or a Ford Focus RS RX for rallycross, because the car with the better engine would win, not the one fine-tuned for specific goals. The weight difference is only noticeable between a truck and a Mini Cooper, slipstreaming is non-existent, detailed damage affecting specific parts of the car (sometimes the car just stops accelerating without any visible reason), and the suspension doesn’t feel realistic at all (play Dirt Rally and you’ll understand what I mean).

3) All possible forces affecting the car while driving don’t apply to the AI, which just drives in a straight line. If you don’t overtake them in one of the first turns, chances are you won’t be able to overtake them at all.

On the plus side, the various events and community interactions are worth mentioning: the ability to share car setups, vinyls, create your own races, weekly events with prizes, ranked races, and more.

The glaring flaws include getting stuck in rocks without being able to get out and the pixelated trees that will catch you while driving through forests. The lack of a reset car button means you have to wait for the game to decide to respawn you after getting stuck, which looks ridiculous, especially in co-op.

Multiplayer - Its existence is certainly commendable, but there’s absolutely no desire to play it. Here’s why:

1) Incredibly long wait times for matchmaking. I played 5 races in an hour and a half, which is unacceptable for online play.

2) This isn’t just a multiplayer problem, but a racing issue in general – checkpoint limitations. The purpose is clear, to prevent cutting half the track, but when you miss a checkpoint by a millimeter and have to go back, it feels absurd.

3) Slowing down when hitting walls. This must have been thought up by someone with the IQ of a loaf of bread. When you hit a wall, you already lose speed and trajectory, but it’s your choice, accepting the consequences of careless driving. Here, the game adds insult to injury by slowing you down even more, just because it wants to. Penalty upon penalty. Bravo.

4) Collisions. The cars just become intangible. Why? What for? Apparently, the same person responsible for the previous point worked on this too.

Graphics - Incredibly beautiful visuals even in 2024. The cars are excellently detailed, including the interiors. Gorgeous landscapes that change with the seasons.

Audio - Super cool music selection for every taste, presented as radio stations. And while there isn’t much for each station, I haven’t gotten tired of a single track in 100 hours. A minor drawback – when switching radio stations, the track doesn’t continue, so you can’t skip a song that doesn’t fit the situation or that you just don’t like. The engine sounds are also pleasing to the ear.

Conclusion - Excellent arcade racing with unnecessary sim elements. The graphics are great, as is the audio. It’s better to avoid multiplayer, and it’s best to download car setups for a more enjoyable experience.

10 car collections out of 10.

For my taste, after more than 3,000 hours I can assure that it is the car game I always dreamed of since I started playing video games in 1986.

It has everything, spectacular graphics and quite good and varied music. With a GTX 1060 and an already outdated i7-3820, it is very well optimized. The video settings are made automatically according to the components, in my case it leaves them in medium rendering quality, which as I say looks very good, and always moving very fluidly at 72 FPS, at 1440p.

The negative point was, and I say was, because I don't know what fixed it, whether Windows 10 updates, or Nvidia updates, I don't know, but the first few months I was desperate because day after day, the game would freeze and then close, even several times a day. It hasn't happened to me for several months now, sometimes sporadically, but very little. If it stays the same, I can say that for me it is a must-buy if you like car games.

Finally, I can say that you can spend hours on whatever you want, racing on roads, mountains, jumping, landing on roofs, etc, making your own tune-ups, which I don't do out of laziness, designing the skins of the cars... well, those 3,000 hours can easily go by if you like to fully customize a car to your liking, and there are 752 cars.

I hope you enjoy it as much as I do, greetings :)


Update: I'm eating my words with potatoes. Today I've already had two game freezes, one when choosing a car and the other when traveling to LEGO. A few days ago I updated Windows with the May patches, that's all I've done. I'm sorry, but if this becomes the general trend again I'll have to change my rating of the game.

Pros: This game is addicting and has lots of content. 
Cons: it shouldn't be 60$ for a 3 year old game

Perhaps there’s no point in reviewing a game that’s no longer possible to purchase on Steam and perhaps there’s even less of a reason for anyone to actually read this in mid 2025 but this game deserves more praise even in the era of “the lack of videogame preservation”.

Forza Horizon 4 is easy to pick up and start playing. It welcomes you to explore, it invites you to mix and try different races, different classes and different activities. There’s a lot to see and do. Plenty of roads to discover (more than 500) beautiful locations that can truly change the way you play it based on the different 4 seasons and a nice selection of radio tunes to keep you company. This is not my first time playing this game, I finished it once and I’m now aiming for another run on PC but this time with the two DLC expansions. I decided to get this game last minute before no longer being able to purchase on Steam and while I’m happy, part of me feels empty to know that this is an incredible game that is not being available to everyone looking for more Forza Horizon in their lives. The game still holds up in pretty much everything, music, visuals, performance and at almost 40 hours I still need to wrap up one of the DLC before going to the next one. There’s so much game in this videogame that truly begs the question what can we do to keep videogame preservation a thing of the present and not just a wish hoping to be true. 

I actually put my backlog cleaning on hold to play this game one more time. Despite no longer being able to purchase on Steam the game lives on. Players are still active, you can still see them cruising, drifting and messaging the lobby with a shy “hi” as if they were trying to keep the memory alive, as well as the game itself. There’s some feeling I can’t describe to see a removed game with an active audience. Players still want to play this game and licenses and contracts put the dream down for good for many others.

Forza Horizon 5 is well and alive but we have to wonder for how long. Forza Horizon 4 is now part of History, a warm memory for some, only a wish to play for others. If you find a way, come and join, the old timers still want to have fun in the lobbies.

[h1]Burnout, Need for Speed and Test Drive Unlimited had a threesome...[/h1]

FH4 is the best arcade racing game. It has a lot content, great selection of cars, fun gameplay, good controls and physics.

I'm extremely happy that Forza Horizon 4 is finally on Steam, I wanted to play this game for years. But xbox app was testing my patience.

It's an open world racing game. I guess by cranking up the difficulty and realism settings you could bring it closer to sim-cade level, but mostly it's arcade, a fun one, where laws of physics still exist and different cars handle differently.

A while ago when there were mainly arcade games on the market I always wanted more simulators or something arcade but which makes sense when it comes to handling. But then the age of simulators started. Sure they're fun, but they're tiring while Forza is relaxing in a way. Well, you can make it relaxing or challenging. It's the most fun racing game on the market.

Car handling is awesome. The weight transfer physics work which is especially useful in dirt racing, you can drift which requires some effort unlike in other games. It's just that awesome feeling, fun and slightly realistic.

Car selection is amazing. Everyone will find a car they adore. There are hundreds of cars, something like 700 maybe? Cars have classes and the selection is very diverse. From vintage cars to modern supercars, from regular road cars to rally cars or even trucks or vans. There are even Lego and hot Wheels cars. Just insane.
Maybe one downside is that you get a bunch of cars really quickly so there's no sense of progression because you're being given the fastest cars in the first hours of the game. I prefer starting with regular cars and make my way up to earn faster, more expensive cars. Fortunately you can choose whatever car in exhibition races but still it lack progression.

So you race in England. At first it's slightly confusing to drive on the wrong lane, of course you can drive however you like but still coming from other games like ETS2 it's a bit confusing, especially the roundabouts. Not in a bad way though.
The map is huge and very diverse. Highways, dirt roads, small roads, forests, mountains, lakes, city, everything you want is there for you to explore. And exploring is fun. There are hidden barns and other collectables. While barns are fun, they give you a new car but other collectables are just there for the sake of...collectables. But again – not a bad thing, some of them are fun to find. One of the fun collectable types are beauty spots. You see a beautiful cut-scene of the area/object.

The game revolves around competing in a festival. There are various challenges which give you rewards when you complete them. Most of the time you'll need to win races but there are other challenges, like speed traps where you must drive as fast as possible or the ones where you need to jump off a ramp and be in the air for as long as possible.
But of course racing is the most important here and you have few types of races. Circuit racing, point A to B racing. But that's not all. There A to B races where you need to follow the road and there are ones where you just need to get to finish line as quick as possible by driving wherever you like, no rules. Team racing where one team competes against drivatar team or other players. There are also races against trains or planes. On top of that there are taxi missions. Which bring us to story events. Those are events/races with some story to it. They're fun and challenging and will keep you occupied for a while.

Now multiplayer activities. Racing is obviously one of them but there's also capture the flag where you must carry the flag to destination and other team needs to stop you. Matches where infected team need to touch other cars to infect them. Protect the king matches which is similar. And the most surprising one – battle royale.
There's also ranked play. It has stricter rules like you can't hit the walls because you get penalized.

But it's not all multiplayer only. Amount of single player content is insane. You can choose to race solo on your chosen difficulty level, a coop race against drivatars and story missions.
The game basically gives you a choice how you want to play it.

You can customize your character and own a house, multiple houses which serve as your garage and home where you can tune your cars and your appearance.
You can also tune your cars accordingly to race you're going to participate. Don't want that? Just download the setup straight from the game. You can apply liveries to your cars by creating your own where the only limit is your imagination or just download a livery.
To get new stuff you spin a fortune wheel and rewards are ranging from money and clothes to some cool cars. You earn wheelspins by playing the game.

You can drive anywhere, hit bushes, smaller trees, rocks, fences – the environment is destructible. But the best part are seasons. There're four seasons which change over time. Each season has its challenges to compete for you. And season changes could even change your driving. On winter it could be harder to drive but lakes are frozen so you can have fun on the lake. Seasons along with dynamic weather change the map drastically.

This is one of the best looking games. Seasons change the map so much that it feels fresh each time. All the seasons are absolutely beautiful.
Cars look amazing and they're all are fully modelled. You can look closely at every part of the car.
Environments look great. Distant objects are lower quality but overall the game looks stunning.
There's also a photo mode where you can take beautiful pictures. But I find most filters pretty poor so it's better to tune the colors by yourself.

When the game looks that good I don't expect it to run smoothly. But this is probably the best performing game currently in my library. Runs on max graphics, 80-100fps, smooth as butter. I'm playing on 5800x, 2070s, 32GB @3440x1440.
There's native ultrawide support. Although cut-scenes are cropped for some reason.

It has a lot of loading screens so I suggest to install this to m.2 ssd. They're usually short, 3 to 15 seconds, but there are so many of them that it gets annoying. It's especially annoying in mp because everyone must wait until the slowest PC will load the game which could take 15 minutes. How fun is it to wait 15 minutes for a 5min race?
I noticed many people complaining about stuttering cut-scenes. But cut-scenes are actually loading screens.

One more minor annoying thing is unskippable voice when you open the map and there's something new on it. It tells you about new activities but after 20th time I just don't want to hear it anymore it's the most annoying thing in the whole game besides clueless online players.

Sound design is perfect. Cars sound great, the festival site feels alive.
There're radio stations so most people will find something to listen to but t lack a metal station.

Overall an extremely good racing game for anyone who at least slightly enjoys racing games. It's great for everyone's taste due to plenty of different activities and modes to play.
I suggest buying the ultimate edition. It only lacks two dlc's. Not at full price obviously.

I’ve always had a soft spot for British cities, towns, villages and countryside. As someone who is a fan of open-world games, and enjoys an arcade racing game now and then, I definitely find [I]Forza Horizon 4[/I] an appealing title. It’s set in a highly condensed, simplified version of central and northern Great Britain that includes Edinburgh, the Scottish Highlands, the Lake District, Ambleside, Broadway, and Bamburgh. This picturesque, yet uncommon, setting for an open-world game, makes [I]FH4[/I] even more special.

Although [I]Forza Horizon 5[/I] was released past November, [I]FH4[/I] is still a relevant game. At the time of this review, the [I]FH4[/I] community is still quite active, with at least 20 players -- sometimes as many as 50 -- online in my sessions. With all additional official content for [I]FH4[/I] having been released, you’ll know exactly what you’ll get when you buy this game. When it comes down to it, your preference in scenery will be the major determining factor in deciding between [I]FH4[/I] and [I]FH5[/I].

[I]FH4[/I] is a playground with plenty of game modes to unlock and access. Aside from an impressive tutorial that guides you through various types of races, terrains, seasons, and weather conditions in the first several minutes, you pretty much have free reins on your driving adventure from the start. The action in [I]FH4[/I] centres on:
[LIST]
[*]story-based challenges called Horizon Stories, with The Stunt Driver and British Racing Green being my favourites;
[*]races (Road, Dirt, Street, Cross Country, and Showcase), with racing/chasing a train in a 1959 Ford Anglia like in [I]Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets[/I] being most memorable;
[*]PR stunts (speed traps and zones, stunt jumps, drifting zones); and
[*]events (live in-game challenges titled Forzathon Live, as well as daily and weekly challenges).
[/LIST]

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2684469342

There is also a battle royale mode called The Eliminator, as well as a series of user-created challenges named Super7. Mechanically inclined players can also tune their vehicles, artistic ones can design liveries for their cars, construction oriented folks can devise new racing routes, and shutterbugs can capture their favourite cars at eye-catching moments using the in-game camera mode. All can share their creations with the [I]FH4[/I] community to enjoy. [I]FH4[/I] has something for everybody regardless of your levels of enthusiasm and skill for driving and racing games. It even offers to adjust the difficulty level based on your recent racing performances.

If you wish, you can simply explore the over 300 roads on the map. I spent my first 30 hours or so mainly doing that, plus triggering speed traps and zones, doing stunt jumps, destroying smashable signs, and seeking and photographing as many of the over 700 featured cars as I could. I’ve truly enjoyed the freedom with which I had just exploring the in-game world by car, without ever worrying about the police, griefers, and dying. This is something that even [I]Grand Theft Auto[/I] couldn’t offer.

If that’s not enough, there are the expansion packs: [I]Fortune Island[/I] and [I]LEGO Speed Champions[/I]. The former transports you to a mountainous island with sheer cliffs and extreme weather, and the latter to the joyful LEGO Valley, where structures are made of LEGO bricks. If you enjoy driving or racing games with challenging terrain and treasure hunting, I think you’ll enjoy [I]Fortune Island[/I]. I recommend [I]LEGO Speed Champions[/I] to all because it’s just so whimsical and delightful to see LEGO vehicles go toe-to-toe against real cars.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2703143656

[I]FH4[/I] employs tricks like endowed progress effect, artificial scarcity, randomized reward, and leaderboards to make gameplay addictive. You’re awarded Skill or Influence Points for almost everything you do. Skill Points convert to Perks for your cars, and Influence Points unlock new races, events and prizes. Winning races and completing events will earn you Credits, which you use to buy new cars and houses. At times, you’ll get the chance to win (rare) prizes in Wheelspins. With these reward systems in place, [I]FH4[/I] is more fun and addictive than I had initially imagined.

Don’t want to wait to win or buy a specific car? You can see if one of the several DLC car packs has it. I decided to buy [I]Forza Horizon 4: Ultimate Edition[/I] mainly because I wanted the [I]LEGO Speed Champions[/I] expansion pack and the Best of Bond Car pack. I don’t regret my decision, for this is the closest I’ll ever get to driving cross Britain in a 1964 Aston Martin DB5, even though it doesn’t come with Q’s enhancements.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2684410944

What keeps [I]FH4[/I] interesting and dynamic after all these hours is that the game changes season every real-time week. Each season comes new events and challenges, such as being able to drag race on a frozen lake in winter. If anything, [I]FH4[/I] has so much content that the game’s menu and map can get overwhelming, and disorienting. It’s one of the game’s few shortcomings. The other is the absence of a custom radio station, which is a real shame since I’d love to play soundtrack from James Bond films as I trek across the land in the DB5.

Playing [I]FH4[/I] has been an entertaining way to bid 2021 farewell, and welcome 2022. At the time of this review, I’ve clocked in just under 80 hours of playing time, and I foresee putting in many more in the weeks to come. Needless to say, I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys open-world games and arcade racing games. While the Ultimate Edition may not be for you, I think the base game and at least a couple of the DLCs are worth checking out.

[h3]⚔️ Gameplay & Exploration: [/h3]

Forza Horizon 4 is set in a beautifully detailed, fictionalized version of Scotland, centered around Edinburgh. The open-world map offers a mix of scenic landscapes, from bustling city streets to serene coastal roads and rolling countryside. The standout feature is the dynamic seasons, which change weekly, affecting both the visuals and gameplay. Whether you’re driving through autumn’s golden forests or tackling icy winter roads, the seasons keep the world feeling fresh and varied.

The game’s wide array of race types—from traditional road races to off-road events—ensures there’s something for every driving style. The diversity encourages you to experiment with different vehicles, whether you prefer high-speed asphalt races or rugged cross-country adventures. It’s this variety that keeps the game engaging over time, always presenting new challenges and experiences.

One memorable feature is the crossover mission with Halo, where you get to drive the Warthog as Master Chief. The mission is a love letter to Halo fans, complete with authentic sound effects, familiar settings, and Covenant ships flying overhead. It’s these unique events that make Forza Horizon 4 more than just a racing game, offering moments that blend gaming worlds in a creative way.

The game offers extensive content for completionists. From seasonal events to rare car unlocks, there’s always something to strive for. The Level 10 races for each type are among the more difficult challenges, especially for those seeking mastery. Additionally, getting 3 stars in drifting zones and other advanced challenges can be tough, demanding precise control and skill. For collectors, the rotating seasons mean you need to stay consistent to grab certain cars and rewards. Additionally, some achievements might require clever workarounds or rolling back your system date if you miss them, so plan accordingly.

[h3][b]Wipes the floor with competition[/b][/h3]
[hr]Ever since I got my license, I refrained from taking mindless drives for a number of reasons. The gas price is steep. Dealers charge exorbitant rates for car parts. And most drivers see themselves as the second coming of Vin Diesel, making roads unsafe. So I had no choice but to satisfy the need in another way—the [b]Forza[/b] way. [b]Playground Games[/b]’ magnum opus is an elysian trip down the roads of the UK, like going full-throttle on a freeway with the radio up and windows down.[hr]
[h3][b]A racing bliss[/b][/h3]
You walk through the entrance. It’s a whole new world, a loud and brash festival for car lovers. Whether you’re here for celebration or competition, there’s a spot for you. The land down under was host to the previous Horizon festival, but this time, it has traveled all the way to the beautiful countryside of Britain. You’re an up-and-coming driver seeking fame, and the festival provides you the means to become one.

[b]Forza Horizon 4[/b] (FH4) is not in pursuit of a full-fledged campaign like the [b]Fast & Furious[/b]-wannabe games, which often sink into tedium. Instead, it comes with wholesome story threads to highlight the vastness of British engineering: the stunt driver, express delivery, and the world’s fastest taxi to name a few. The remaining ones, however, are designed more elegantly. A famous vlogger, for example, invites you to take iconic cars from other racing games out for a spin. A documentary that covers the automotive culture and history of Great Britain is in production, and you’re summoned to put cars from classics to modern-day beasts through their paces.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2542406438
[h3][b]United Kingdom? No. Your kingdom[/b][/h3]
One look at the game’s map might have you thinking it’s big but not too big for the reputation of the franchise, though once your foot is on the pedal, everything is bound to change. You are free to drive as you please, and there are no stone-hard walls or invisible barriers to slow you down. It is a seamless world shared between its multiplayer and single-player. You can play it absolutely offline if you want, too.

You’re not forced to make ends meet by driving a single car until your wallet is heavy enough to afford a better one. Thankfully, a whopping number of vehicles—752 to be exact—are on the catalog to be obtained via different methods. Be it offered gratis, awarded for finishing weekly challenges, won in an auction, or earned through a wheelspin system as you progress further, it’s stellar indeed to have such a vast array of classic autos, retro machines, offroad monsters, and hypercars all at once.

But what made the series so special since its first debut? It is the vibrant world and excellent SimCade experience it offers. I’m neither a gearhead nor have driven anything but a Peugeot 206, though I can tell the feel when the rubber meets the road is done delicately. Whether using stock automobiles or finely-tuned ones, the racing remains peerless. The arcade handling ensures the game is accessible to new racers, while the heed to technicalities such as weight, speed, and torque gives it a personality beyond any recent racing titles.

It is also considered a haven for drift junkies. The art of carefully losing control of your car, as some might say. In addition to natural-born drifters, Hoonigan and Formula Drift should be your go-to cars for oversteering. However, with heavy tinkering, any machine can pull off the sideways action. It's a technical challenge that I've yet to master, but the very few times I managed to do so were glorious.

After the prologue, a wide range of activities pops out of every nook and cranny, though it isn’t only relegated to street racing. There are many instances of cross-country and rally competitions. Exploration is also presented in an engaging way: whizzing by speed cameras or pulling off slick stunts both yield hefty amounts of XP, while the game encourages wildlife and car photography as a hobby. Feel free to bring your friends along, challenge others to PVP, or take on the Drivatars. Speaking of which, much of my criticism stems from the fact that AI drivers turn without penalty in slippery conditions and often outpower you despite their lower-performance vehicles. At other times, the AI gives up entirely by crashing into the environment and never coming back.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2542409403
Would it be surprising to say [b]Forza[/b] has a Battle Royale mode too? Not at all since those games have taken over the mantle. However, despite my simmering hatred of BRs, The Eliminator mode is rather enjoyable. Luck is not the primary decider, as you'll always have a chance to win even in low-tier vehicles. You have to ferociously race players head to head while securing better cars.

As for the cherry on top, the Horizon festival takes you through a tour of the four seasons, rotating on a weekly basis with new challenges each time. It’s not just the world turning into shades of amber and red as the autumn arrives or white when the snowfall hits; it takes on an entirely new identity. Your favorite gas guzzlers become a paperweight on icy roads unless correct parts like tires, to name one, are applied.

It’s all good fun until you decide to show off your mastery in online races. Reportedly, FH4 on Steam is inferior to the Microsoft Store version in terms of stability and connectivity. While I was burning rubber at a rock-solid 60 FPS, with settings cranked down to medium on a [I]Ryzen 5 3500X, GTX 1050 2GB, and 16 GB RAM[/i], many others were unfortunate to experience constant crashes or stutters. Anyway, no matter if I was racing in a free-for-all playlist or competing in ranked leagues, matchmaking issues and prolonged loading times due to players leaving mid-game left a bitter taste in my mouth. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn’t.

[h3][b]’Tis the season for therapeutic music and drive[/b][/h3]
[b][u]Visuals[/u][/b]
Virtual Great Britain may not be the most precise presentation of it seen to date but, oh my, isn’t it stunning nonetheless. The shifts in seasons ensure you see it all: dirt, ice, and tarmac. From ripping through sprawling flower fields in spring to the crunch of dry, dead leaves beneath your tires in fall, it makes a [i]jolly[/i] good spectacle, come rain or shine.

But what is greater than Britain? It’s the cars. They are rendered meticulously and are almost indistinguishable from their real-life models. The obsessive attention to detail, both interior and exterior, is too good of a photoshoot opportunity to pass.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2542410911
[b][u]Audio[/u][/b]
The countryside is peaceful at all times, but the rumble of a turbocharged flat-four is the only noise that disturbs the tranquility of rural life. Pop, indie, R&B, rap, and other blasting tunes are all here to liven up the festival. Have a rather tender soul? Timeless FM has got you covered. Take that Jaguar E-Type out of the garage, listen to classics from Beethoven, Brahms, and Mozart while cruising through Edinburgh like you’re here only for the culture—or a cup of tea. Others say the soundscape lacks authenticity compared to its predecessor. It may do, but I have yet to play that.

[h3][b]The bottom line[/b][/h3]
[hr]Given the top-notch graphics and abundant activities, FH4 is an incredible SimCade with a satisfying loop of fun and rewards. It sets itself miles ahead of its competitors. It’s not the perfect racing experience, but then again it’s not trying to be. It’s a sophisticated, effortless luxury.[hr]

[b]Forza Horizon 4 delivers that perfect balance of arcade fun and realistic driving that reminds me why I love open-world racing games. It’s got that thrilling sense of freedom, whether you're racing through scenic British countryside or just cruising down the coast with the wind in your hair. The game is packed with content, offering everything from chaotic street races to chill drives through dynamic seasons that completely change the game’s landscape. It keeps the action fast and the vibes high.

The car collection is absolutely fantastic—there’s something for every kind of driver, from classic muscle cars to hypercars, and each one handles beautifully in the game’s seamless world. The progression system is smooth, and there’s always something new to work toward, whether it’s unlocking a new car or completing challenges. The seasonal changes are a standout feature, giving the game a fresh feeling every week and keeping you coming back to see how the environment changes. Plus, the racing itself feels tight, with just the right amount of challenge without feeling overly punishing.

Visually, the game is jaw-dropping. From the stunning textures on the cars to the breathtaking landscapes, it’s a visual feast for any racing fan. The soundtrack is killer too, pumping up the adrenaline with a solid mix of tunes that complement the high-speed action. Multiplayer is a blast, and while the AI isn’t perfect, it provides solid competition for solo players.

That said, Forza Horizon 4 does have a couple of minor issues. Sometimes, the rubber-banding AI can feel frustrating, especially during tight races, and there’s the occasional hiccup with car collisions or environmental objects that don’t always behave as expected. The microtransactions aren’t overbearing, but it’s still something to consider if you're looking for a completely free experience.

All in all, Forza Horizon 4 is a spectacular racing game that combines accessibility with depth. If you love driving games that allow you to explore vast open worlds and race at your own pace, Forza Horizon 4 is one of the best in the genre. Despite a few small annoyances, it’s an adrenaline-packed, visually stunning ride that’s hard to put down.[/b]

[b]Perfect Buy-in Time for this Gem![/b]

If you're like me and eyeballing the new Forza 5, don't overlook the most recent predecessor. Four is on sale now at 65% off for everything. I've not had it too long, and it still has a lot of replay value. It's the best racing game I've ever played, hands down.  Now is the best time to buy in at these sale prices. I like the fact that you can enjoy the game, even if you are not one of the better racers. There's a lot of crash-em-up fun as well.

Let me start by saying that Forza is not a terrible game by any means and it's not "broken" or anything close to that.
That being said, I think this game doesn't get enough criticism and it might mislead some people about it. It's the kind of game that might charm you at first but the more you play it, the more the tons of minor annoyances start to pile up and ruin the experience.

[b] I'll start with the good things : [/b]
-It looks good and it runs well. Performance and visuals are rarely and issue and as long as you have an alright machine you are probably not gonna have any problem trying to run it at 60 fps or above. 
-Car selection is unmatched. You won't ever find a game with this amount of cars in any other place.
-Plenty of content and a decent open world to drive in.
-It's pretty decent for arcade racers and for people looking for a slightly more realistic driving experience.

So as a racing game in general, you know, it's pretty fine. It checks the boxes of driving decently, looking good and having plenty to do.

[b]Now, my issues with it...[/b]

-Bland. This is subjective, I know, but it can get quite irritating. This blandness is all over the game. The dialogues, characters, stories, visuals, music... everything is as non-offensive and PG-friendly as possible to a fault. I don't expect it to be super edgy or something but, it just lacks any real personality at all.

-I hope you like listening to the same 4-5 songs in each loading screen because that's all you will have for the rest of your experience. And don't worry, you can't mute them either because music can't be fully turned off.

-Despite what you may have seen or read here, playing with a steering wheel sucks. I have the very common Logitech G29 and the Force Feedback is basically non existent and feels really odd. You are just putting yourself in a disadvantage if you actually wanna play with a wheel. It's extremely jarring coming from Assetto Corsa (A sim, I know, but still). Maybe fine for casual use but if you have tried more serious racing games, wheel implementation is bad. The game is definitely optimized for controllers first, then keyboard, and steering wheel last.

-There is more loading than you would expect. For example, The Crew despite being a worse game, lets you fast travel teleport and go around the world seamlessly. Here basically everything has a loading screen, a short one, but there is one. Considering how "optimized" and modern this game is, it's a rather disappointing aspect of it and affects the flow of the game.

-[b]Online is absolute garbage[/b]. Trying to make a convoy with friends? Fine, that probably works...sometimes. Now don't even try to join a race together because the process tends to be convoluted and end up with someone disconnected. Now, if you actually manage to join a race or event pray that the rest of the people actually connect to it. If you are lucky enough you will be able to play some. Otherwise, you are probably gonna get stuck at some loading screen for literal 10 minutes while the game tries to find or synchronize players.
It's just, awful. Absolutely pathetic that a game this modern can't figure out a proper online system that doesn't suck like this. It's barely functional sometimes and it really blows my mind how you can be waiting for 10 or more minutes trying to do something without even the option to cancel the loading so you have to straight up close the game.

-Sound. Already addressed some in FH5 but, the sound in this game can go from quite alright to straight up bad, really bad. From inaccurate sounds, to very artificial ones. There are some quite decent ones mind you but it's very subpar compared to other racing titles. Basically any NFS game that you have played will have more exciting car sounds than this and that is quite sad.

-The hand holding. If you wanna "progress" through the story of the game be prepared to be interrupted all the time with dialogues and more dialogues telling you what to do next and where to go.

-The intro section is so long too, it takes a couple of hours before you can actually get into the real game, and you have to go every season before getting into the real festival, and proper multiplayer. I understand kinda why they did it like that but the game isn't that complex and having to jump through so many hoops to actually get into the real thing is just annoying.

-Lack of progression, despite being part of the core philosophy of the game is a bit boring. Since you are able to basically do whatever you want with whatever car you want in the game, getting new cars doesn't really feel rewarding and finishing events through the game just doesn't feel too special. Some people might prefer this sandbox style but I admit I prefer a more old-school kind of progression through the game.

-Wheelspins. Be ready to waste time and expectations collecting emotes, horn sounds, awful clothes and absolutely useless 2.000 credits prizes. -Ads. I can't believe a game of this price actually has unskipable ads in it. -Quick chat is a neat feature that's again, ruined by only being able to equip 4 at the same time which basically means that it's impossible to communicate properly with other people in the world. This game just doesn't feel made to be "social", ironically.

Those are basically my thoughts. First off, I am going to get this out of the way. If you are planning to buy this game and wondering which version to get, ask yourself this. If you are a minimalist, standard is fine. If you want the expansions, get ultimate. Deluxe on the other hand I think is worth skipping entirely. If $99.99 is too much for you for Ultimate, just wait for a sale. Ultimate is definitely my choice for recommendation. The amount of content you get is impressive and worth the price of admission. 

Forza Horizon 4 is a car collector's dream, with a roster of over 700 cars (with Ultimate). And also a racing enthusiasts dream playground with a decently sized map with tons of racing variety and events to play around with. I have tons of racing games on Steam personally, and none have held my interest as much as Forza Horizon 4. It's a shame though that this came so late to Steam. But even still, I got my money's worth with over 120 hours of playtime at the time of writing this. 

Is Forza Horizon 4 perfect though? Sadly, it is not. The Steam version is hampered with some unfortunate bugs. People may experience random crashes, which while not happening often after the last few updates, still do happen, as this game is a few versions behind the Microsoft store's own version. Something I don't know if will ever be fully fixed. Also online racing can be hit or miss with issues. Those issues usually lie in the wait times sadly, so it might be offputting for those looking to race with others. Luckily there is more than enough content without having to do online races to keep most people happy. 

 I'm still giving this a recommend regardless of that issue, just because more often than not, the game does run smoothly. 

If you happen to just get the standard version of the game you get access to the main map which is a caricatured version of Great Britain, which includes many race events ranging from your standard street races, dirt tracks and even full blown off road events. There are also other events which include speed traps, drifting, massive jumps, promotional events (like racing the Halo Warthog, racing against trains, and more), and some cool little story events like racing for Top Gear, or even opening your own businesses. There's plenty of content for sure. If you decide to get the expansions, you get other maps, including Fortune Island, which is, well, an Island, complete with both low and high altitude locations, lots of off roading, some impressive night time visuals (Aurora Borealis anyone?), and more. You also get the Lego Speed Champions map which is a fun and impressively designed map based on the Lego toys which features it's own variety of fun and unique settings, including a beach riddled with pirate ships, a haunted lighthouse, a stunt arena, and more. Also it gets it's own radio station that plays just 1 song on loop. If you guessed that song is "Everything is Awesome", you'd be right, Both expansions also come with a unique way of progression and their own vehicles to collect. Fortune Island will have you progress to unlock a variety of treasure hunts, that each unlock 1 million credits, and the Lego expansion has you doing different tasks to collect studs which can be used to build your house and also collect new cars. Both expansions will also include a majority of the types of events you will be used to in the base game, with their own unique flair. 

With 700 cars luckily there is enough variety for anyone. But for those looking for more, you can custom tune each vehicle to your own liking, with a variety of parts and overhauls, including full blown engine swaps. For those who are not gear heads, the community has you covered and you can even download custom tunes from others. Forza Horizon 4 is one of the most generous racing games I have ever played with the sheer amount of cars they dump on you. You can win cars from events. You can win cars from wheelspins. you can win cars from leveling up. You can win cars from performing certain tasks. You can win cars from barn finds, which are like little treasure hunts. You can also buy cars from both an auto show, or take your chances at an in game auction house, which is also a great way to make money, to well, buy more cars. Basically, Horizon does not let you down with the cars. It's like Pokemon for car lovers. And once you have that dream car, don't forget to give it that unique look. Most cars can have some visual parts swapped out, ranging from spoilers to bumpers and more, and you can add custom designs to the paint jobs too. Want to race around in Jurassic Park Jeep? Want to race around in the Bandit 1 from Smokey and the Bandit? Forza has you covered. And if you just want to look at the cars in all their glory, Forza also has a nice little feature called Forzavista which allows to do things with your car like opening and closing doors, and for some vehicles you can open up trunks and hoods and look inside at the engines. If you get the James Bond pack, you can even look at those nifty little gadgets like the machine guns mounted to some of the Bond vehicles. Pretty neat stuff. 

At the end of the day, is Forza Horizon 4 worth it? I'd say yes.

The UK is not exactly famous for its wonderful roads, but there are no two-hour traffic jams on the M25 or dispiriting stretches of the North Circular in Forza Horizon 4’s Britain. This is the Britain of romantic comedies, postcards and, one presumes, Brexiteers’ imaginations. It is an idealised, compressed representation of our island comprising the Cotswolds, the Lake District, acres of beautiful woodland, the Highlands, Edinburgh, the east coast and the moors. There’s no urban sprawl, no rubbish suburbs and, perhaps most attractively of all, barely any people. In Forza Britain, instead of toiling in the gig economy to make your extortionate rent, you are gifted a house for helping out with some stunts on a movie shoot.

The game even turns our weather into something beautiful. As the seasons change, so does the climate and the nature of the light, along with the driving conditions. Edinburgh’s New Town shimmers in pale spring sunshine, and in winter the snow in the Highlands sucks all the light out of the sky. The cottages in Ambleside are prettiest in the summer, when the trees are so bracingly green you can almost smell them. If you have a 4K television, this is what it was made for. Now and then, such as the first time I drove past Edinburgh Castle in the perfect twilit blue of a summer night in Scotland, its beauty made me quite emotional.

The way all the cars feel are completely unique, and very close to reality. You can feel the weight of a Lamborghini, and you can feel the differences in shifting gears and precision between all cars. All of that is pure perfection. The graphics and sound is great too.

This is obviously very subjective, but here’s my review.  Spoiler Alert: 9.5/10 from me.

Overview:
I was a PlayStation gamer for many years prior to branching out to PC gaming a few years ago, so I never got to experience the Forza games until recently.  Forza Horizon 5 was my introduction to the series.  I really enjoyed it and scored it an 8/10 in my Steam review.  I then decided to try out Forza Horizon 4, and I just love it, can’t get enough.  FH4 is a fantastic game and far superior to FH5 in my opinion.  

Driving / Difficulty:
I generally opt for more simulator-type driving games, i.e. realistic driving.   It’s safe to say that this game definitely does not fall in to that category, instead leaning more towards the arcade style... there’s nothing wrong with that at all!  There are 8 difficulty (Drivatar) levels to choose from, ranging from from new player to unbeatable.  This allows the game to cater to most skill levels… unless you’re either really bad, or play like Jarno Opmeer or SuperGT (lucky you!!).  There’s also a huge amount of assists which you can opt for, such as, auto transmission, TCR, STM, ABS, assisted steering, assisted braking, damage on/off, tyre wear on/off, and driving line.  Whatever way you choose to play is up to you, but there are options to suit almost everyone.  

Gameplay:
The FH4 world is outstandingly beautiful.  The landscape is stunning, and I love how it changes through the seasons.  The attention to detail in the world design is superb.  The story was… meh.  Not memorable, with some very tedious moments and a few non-skippable cutscences.  But it was more interesting that FH5’s story imo.  The game has heaps self-contained storylines and businesses too which are fun, a nice challenge, and encourage you to explore parts of the map you may not otherwise experience.  There's a vast range of cars to earn (~500) by completing various races, events, stories, accolades etc.  You can also win cars, money, cosmetic items etc. through Wheelspins.  The game is very generous with how easy Wheelspins are to earn, especially when compared with how stingy many other game series can be.  Cars can be customised via upgrades and tuning options.  These are great to experiment with to find the right set-up for your favourite cars and to fine tune to suit specific types of races.  I love this feature personally, but for those who don't, there's also a feature that allows tunes made by other members of the community be downloaded.  You can also create your own paintjobs and liveries with infinite possibilities.  There’s endless amounts of stuff to do, along with seasonal (weekly) championships, challenges, and events.  I haven’t even mentioned all the PvP and user-created challenges - people's creativity will never cease to amaze me.  You’ll never be bored!!  After a hard day at work / uni, it's just nice (therapeutic even!) to drive around like a complete lunatic destroying fences, trees, drifting, racing at stupidly high speed, doing massive jumps etc. all while earning points and combos to gain fast XP.  It's even more fun with friends!  The tracks are decent and offer lots of variety in racing styles from drifting to cross-country to circuit to rally.  

Performance:
I run everything on max settings, and FH4 genuinely looks phenomenal.  A number of the negative reviews I've read mention issues with performance.  The game runs fine for me, with just a couple of minor stuttering issues and one or two freezes in ~100 hours of gameplay.  I’ve had no connection issues to friends / other players either.

TL;DR – FANTASTIC game if you're looking for a fun, open-world driving experience.  Lots of styles of racing and tonnes of cars to choose from.  Looks incredible.  Lots to do.  9.5/10 for the fun factor.

Forza Horizon 4 is a game that I got as an impulse purchase of sorts. I was vaguely familiar with the franchise when, in 2024, I learned that this game was going to be delisted. Not only that, some achievements would become unobtainable as they'd be ending seasonal content for it. So, wanting to have delisted games for preservation, and being an achievement hunter, I decided to buy it.

Now, I'll say that I've always enjoyed racing games, but when I got FH4, I tried it for a couple minutes, found it somewhat interesting, but didn't pay much attention until the final Seasonal Playlist (the seasonal content that got discontinued) started. For four weeks, I played every single day in order to get all the related achievements to that mode, and afterwards... I just kept playing, every day. I was hooked, unknowingly, as every day I'd launch the game and play one or two races, do some challenges, work towards getting a cool car. So, why did I get so personally invested in the game, to the point that I'm waiting in anticipation for Forza Horizon 6? In short: lots and lots of cars.

See, the main draw in Forza Horizon 4 seems to be collecting cars, and that's something I've always enjoyed in racing games since playing the original Need for Speed: Most Wanted (the 2005 one). While some people might argue that the game constantly throwing cars at you is a downside (you can get supercars in the first hour!), I personally loved it. After all, it's not like after getting a supercar you can just win every single race; each car has a specific class it belongs to, and races are usually divided by class. Beyond car class, there's also different types of races, which might require specific types of cars: there's Road Racing, Dirt Racing, Cross Country, Drag Racing and even Street Racing (aka, illegal racing, with traffic on the streets; although no cops, this is no NFS). You can even create your own tracks with your own settings, although they must always begin from one of the existing racing spots.

The map, given that this is an open world game, is rather large. Set in a scaled down version of Great Britain, there's several small towns to visit, as well as Edinburgh as the "main" city of the game. Beyond that, there's lots of fields to explore, although obviously, you might prefer driving on roads, and there's lots of them. As I got the Ultimate Edition, my version of the game also had Fortune Island and Lego Valley as two separate maps to explore, with their own events. Speaking of events, beyond the races I mentioned in the previous paragraphs, there's several "PR events" that you can complete, like Drift Zones, Speed Traps and Jumps, to mention a few.

Customization is quite extensive, as you can apply your own liveries to cars, or use one of the thousands already made and shared by other players. Speaking of player generated content, there's custom challenges in the form of the Super7. This aspect of the game, I'm not entirely sold on. While I found some pretty fun challenges along the way, there's many that are extremely simple in terms of design, not necessarily in difficulty, which might make for a boring journey through a Super7 series.

All races can be done either against the AI or against other players, and that's not the only multiplayer option the game offers, as there's the "Adventure" mode, in which you can compete with and against other players in team-based modes. For Battle Royale enthusiasts, the Eliminator mode is basically that, but with cars, as you get dropped into whichever spot you select on the map, and must scout the area for better car drops and other players to eliminate in Head-to-Head races.

Now, as I keep writing this review, I realize it isn't very useful now considering the game is no longer available for purchase, but I just wanted to share how much I enjoyed this game, to the point that I'm eagerly awaiting for Forza Horizon 6. This game's graphics already impressed me, with some very detailed cars; I can't even imagine what the newest entry in the franchise will be like (and the trailers make it look pretty). And the upcoming FH6 is pretty much why I'm writing this review, as it finally gave me the push to finally go for 100% completion in this game.

Forza Horizon 4 (FH4) is an open-world arcade racing game. Initially you are given a few cars and must complete a number of events to progress to the next season. Completing the latter grants you credits to buy more cars and opens up new events, such as street races, off-road trails, online team events, speed traps, jump stunts and even a battle-royal mode with The Governator as a rare announcer. Players may unlock more than 700 cars and may also tune and paint each of them. So you may apply your favorite "Hello Kitty" or "SpongeBob" design on your Hypercar or Truck. FH4 offers so much content in fact that after spending nearly 150 hours, I still have not yet seen everything.

It's interesting that it took the developers from Playground Games quite a while to decide to place Horizon in their homeland, the UK.
After the game wows you with its typically bloated introduction, where all the seasons change within ten minutes, the introductory five-hour familiarization session begins. During it, you will learn how unlocking new plants works, what you need to do to increase your popularity, try out the role of a movie stuntman, buy your first house and, in short, somehow naturally understand the laws of this world.
After those roughly five hours, however, another change will occur - the Horizon festival will break out in full. At that moment, the game will start to follow instructions from the central server, which controls the changes of the seasons. The change occurs every week, is accompanied by a short loading and brings with it a fundamental transformation of the visuals and gameplay. And although thanks to the shared world you will meet other players on the roads and you can simply challenge them to a duel, there is still a full-fledged single player as before.

Changing the seasons is yet another step towards creating a more believable virtual world. As an introduction, I bought a BMW M5 (E60) and parked it next to my new lakeside house. It was just autumn, colorful leaves were rolling on the ground and the surrounding landscape could not have represented the English countryside better – melancholy moors, winding roads on the hillsides, flocks of sheep grazing in the meadows… and then winter came. And I found out that the lake near the house had frozen over, so I could go across it to the opposite shore, which of course was not possible in the summer.

The developers from Playground Games know well how to keep players entertained. The race alternates with the race, mixed in with side activities (like the well-known search for wrecks in barns) or driving mini-games, thanks to which you become, for example, a movie stuntman.

The races themselves are then divided into several categories. There are classic urban circuits, "illegal" night sprints, off-road races, cross-country tracks and a few others.
Horizon 4 still brings a kind of "life simulator" to the festival, but it's a rather grandiose name for a few minor additions. In reality, this means that you can dress up the character, you can see him in various cutscenes, and last but not least, you can also buy cottages, houses, villas, and if you save up a seriously large amount of money, you can get Edinburgh Castle.

There are also two large DLCs in the game.
The first major expansion is aptly named Fortune Island. There's sure to be plenty of riches in the new map inspired by the islands in the north of Britain, but only if you're lucky. The new island will throw you into strong storms, the lightning of which will literally throw trees under your wheels. But once the skies clear, you'll be rewarded with breathtaking aurora borealis, new cars and a new (drift) story.

The second major expansion for Forza Horizon 4 is another of the series' interesting collaborations. Once you could beat the clock on the famous Top Gear circuit, sit in Hot Wheels cars and now a new piece of land in Britain will be transformed into Lego.
DLC Lego Speed Champions adds a new area to Forza with a desert full of dinosaur skeletons, a beach with pirate ships, an amusement park, a city, and a new racing circuit. Everything is in the spirit of Lego. Lego vehicles are also a matter of course.
A total of 250 challenges await you, from regular races to many jumps to breaking Lego creations. Completing the challenges earns you Lego bricks, which you can use to improve your new house, thereby increasing your garage capacity, and this in turn gives you access to new Lego vehicles.

Fun, adrenaline and rewards are dosed with incredible efficiency, and at the same time, the developers successfully avoid problems in the form of loot boxes, grind and similar "conveniences". In this respect, Forza Horizon 4 is almost old-school, and that's a good thing. There is still something to discover, there is still something to spend money on, and the game generously supplies you with more and more rewards for completed races or performed tricks. [b] 95% [/b]

I'm not really a racing-type guy, but after hearing the game's delisting and seeing the whopping 80% off the price tag, I couldn't resist buying this. Oh boi, I'm so glad I did.

After spending a decent amount of time in-game, let me tell you about the experience fellow steam-lurker, because I've been there. I've seen the craziness, from the depths of the deepest lake to the top of the highest mountain, and I can assure you there's no game series like this on the market currently. (No, not even the Crew. Even if it could come close, shittysoft would rather have their entire workforce search for the one black guy mentioned in Japanese history to make him a samurai in their next game, rather than put up a tiny patch to make their older game work offline. The moral of the story: don't overeat snails ppl or you'll lose brain cells.)

Upon starting the game you'll be arriving in the most extensive sandbox I've ever seen. After doing the few "tutorial" races you'll pretty much left to your own devices, like when your mama went to talk to the neighbor Sarah for two minutes and hasn't come home for half a day. The game expects you to do the same stuff you did back then: go crazy and do whatever you want.

Want to explore? 
Enjoy the vast sandbox, especially with the Ultimate edition's add-on packs. You might even come across some very social players and tackle the content in a group co-op session, or just some random fellow weebs to band together and share waifu liveries with each other. I've already seen more tofu drivers drifting off cliffs in this game than anywhere else in my entire life.

Are you more into competition?
Hop into PVP and have the most immersive Balkan driveway experience you could ever wish for. I shit you not, the only thing missing from the complete experience is the random players jumping out of their cars with baseball bats to whoop your arse. It's also a great learning tool, you'll be able to curse in at least ten different languages in no time if you're in the EU.
That's not all, if you have a fortnite-junkie kid you may cure their addiction by making them play elimination. It's a win-win situation if you ask me.

Completionist should also have a great time here with more than 750 cars to collect and tune, not to mention the outworld activities like smashing boards, jump-spots or the Forzathon which is a grand overworld co-op mode.

Overall I really enjoy this game, and sure as heck I'll buy into FH5 one day, when I'm done with this installment. If you decide to grab it, buy the Ultimate, the extra content in it is well worth the 6 bucks.

I've been wanting to play this game since 2019 but I could not afford the PC or the game itself to do so, but now..... even at it's near end of it's run, I'm glad I was able to experience it.

It's not perfect by any means but it's a hell lot of fun, and seeing the backlash Forza Horizon 5 is getting it definitely proves it! But with FH2 and FH1 having their servers shut down, and potentially FH3, I'm sad that in a few years this game will also meet the same fate.

8/10

I have a love-hate relationship with this game. On one hand it's the most fun simcade driving game that I've had the pleasure of playing over the last few years, with hours upon hours of content, amazing graphics, and a really good car selection.

On the other, it's straight up THE most miserable multiplayer experience I have ever had with any game in my life.

Case 1: At it's worst, you can wait up to 15 MINUTES to get into one match, which takes lasts like 3 to 7 minutes at most. And THEN the game might just spontaneously crash whenever it feels like it. It seems to have gotten better since the Steam launch

Case 2:
I wasn't able to play with my friends (who bought the game on the Microsoft Store) for 3 WEEKS because the DNS servers were down, and any support tickets were marked as "answered" even if the issue wasn't solved. Instead of actually fixing the problem, which was clearly on their end, their support deflected instead and put the blame on the players themselves. Only when the servers went down completely and enough people started complaining about it (after 2 weeks since the issue has started) they actually started doing something, and even then, it took them one week straight to actually fix the problem.

Treat this review as a "neutral rating", since Steam doesn't have that option.
Ultimately, the core gameplay is so much fun that I would still highly recommend this game if you're into racing games. Just don't set your expectations for the multiplayer aspect of this game too high because you're just going to end up as disappointed as I am.
